questions.question: What does @SpringBootTest do and when should you use it?
questions.title: @SpringBootTest Purpose and Usage
questions.direct_answer: **@SpringBootTest** asks Spring Boot to create an ApplicationContext through SpringApplication for an integration test. It can discover the main Boot configuration and apply auto-configuration, but the beans and external connections actually created still depend on profiles, properties, mocks, exclusions, and webEnvironment. Use it when the behavior needs broad Boot wiring; use a plain unit test or a slice when that smaller boundary is enough.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that @SpringBootTest boots the whole context and know the cost trade-off versus slice tests and unit tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest for isolated logic that could be tested without starting a Spring context
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention specific webEnvironment modes and explain you prefer @WebMvcTest or @DataJpaTest for slice testing when possible

sections.title: What @SpringBootTest Does and Why It Exists
sections.content:
@SpringBootTest is Spring Boot's broad integration-test annotation. It asks **SpringApplication** to create the Boot application context and can discover the main **@SpringBootApplication** or **@SpringBootConfiguration** class.

It does not promise a production-identical system or force every possible bean and external service to start. The beans, profiles, properties, test doubles, excluded auto-configurations, and web environment still determine what is created. Use it when the test needs several real Spring layers or when you need to verify Boot configuration and wiring. For isolated Java logic, use plain JUnit; for one framework layer, prefer a focused test slice.

sections.title: @SpringBootTest at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|Boot context|~Uses SpringApplication|main Boot configuration|eligible beans and auto-config|test-selected environment
blue|Use it for|~Broad integration checks|several real layers|wiring and configuration|application smoke tests
rose|Trade-off|~More setup than a unit test|cost depends on the app|cache compatible contexts|measure the suite
amber|Narrower options|~Use the smallest boundary|plain JUnit for logic|@WebMvcTest for MVC|@DataJpaTest for JPA

sections.title: Basic @SpringBootTest Integration Test
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @SpringBootTest for every test**: A full Boot context is unnecessary for a pure function or a class whose collaborators can be supplied directly.
- **Confusing MOCK with a running server**: The default mode does not open a listening HTTP port. Use RANDOM_PORT or DEFINED_PORT for a real socket.
- **Assuming automatic cleanup**: Database changes are not rolled back merely because a test uses @SpringBootTest. Use a test-managed transaction where appropriate, or clean state explicitly. Remember that work committed in another thread, such as a real HTTP server request, is outside the test method's transaction.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Boot integration context** — @SpringBootTest creates a context through SpringApplication and applies eligible Boot configuration.
- **Choose the boundary** — use it when the test genuinely needs broad Spring wiring, not for isolated Java logic.
- **Variable cost** — startup time depends on the application and environment; measure instead of relying on a fixed number.
- **Context caching** — the TestContext framework can reuse contexts with the same cache key within the same process.
- **webEnvironment modes** — MOCK, RANDOM_PORT, DEFINED_PORT, and NONE decide whether and how the web environment starts.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: @SpringBootTest creates a Boot application context for an integration test. It can find the main Boot configuration and apply auto-configuration, so it is useful when several real application layers or Boot's wiring are part of the behavior being checked. What actually starts still depends on the test's profiles, properties, mocks, exclusions, and webEnvironment, so it is not automatically identical to production. The default MOCK mode does not open a real HTTP port; RANDOM_PORT does. Because a broad context has more setup than a unit test or slice, I use the smallest test boundary that can prove the behavior. Spring can cache compatible contexts, so unnecessary configuration differences and @DirtiesContext reduce reuse.

questions.question: What are the webEnvironment options for @SpringBootTest and when do you use each?
questions.title: @SpringBootTest webEnvironment Options
questions.direct_answer: **MOCK** is the default: it creates a web ApplicationContext when the classpath supports one, without starting an embedded server, and servlet applications can add MockMvc. **RANDOM_PORT** starts a server on an available port; **DEFINED_PORT** starts it on the configured port; **NONE** creates a non-web context. The client can be TestRestTemplate, WebTestClient, or another suitable client.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of @SpringBootTest configuration beyond just using the defaults, and which client tool pairs with which mode
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing these options exist and then wondering why TestRestTemplate doesn't work with the default MOCK mode
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that RANDOM_PORT prevents port conflicts in CI and mention DEFINED_PORT as an option for debugging

sections.title: Understanding webEnvironment Configuration Options
sections.content:
The **webEnvironment** value controls whether a Spring Boot test creates a web application context and whether it starts an embedded server. **MOCK** is the default: it creates a mock web context when web APIs are available but opens no network port. Servlet tests can add MockMvc. **RANDOM_PORT** starts a server on an available port, **DEFINED_PORT** starts one on the configured port, and **NONE** uses a non-web application context.

Choose the client separately. TestRestTemplate normally calls a running server. WebTestClient can call a server, but it can also bind directly to supported application infrastructure without a real socket.

sections.title: Four webEnvironment Modes at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|MOCK|~Default, no server port|mock web context when supported|servlet tests can add MockMvc|not a socket test
emerald|RANDOM_PORT|~Server on an available port|TestRestTemplate or HTTP client|@LocalServerPort exposes it|avoids a fixed-port clash
amber|DEFINED_PORT|~Server on configured port|real HTTP|use only when fixed port matters|can clash in parallel runs
rose|NONE|~Non-web context|jobs and listeners|no web application context|still loads selected Boot configuration

sections.title: Step 1: Choose Based on What You're Testing
sections.content: Use **MOCK** when no listening server is required; in a servlet application, combine it with @AutoConfigureMockMvc when a broad-context MockMvc test is appropriate. Use **RANDOM_PORT** when the socket, server configuration, filters, and HTTP client path are part of the test. Use **NONE** when the application behavior under test does not require a web application context. Use **DEFINED_PORT** only when the configured port itself matters, since a fixed port can conflict with another process or parallel test.

sections.title: MOCK vs RANDOM_PORT in Practice
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using a network client with MOCK**: MOCK does not open a listening server. Use MockMvc/WebTestClient against the mock context, or choose a port mode for real HTTP.
- **Hard-coding the random port**: An injected TestRestTemplate can use relative paths with its configured root URL. If another client builds an absolute URL, read the actual port with @LocalServerPort.
- **Choosing DEFINED_PORT without isolation**: A fixed port can collide when test processes run in parallel. Use it only when that exact port is part of the requirement and the environment reserves it.
- **Omitting DEFINED_PORT from the model**: It is a fourth option beside MOCK, RANDOM_PORT, and NONE.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **MOCK (default)** — creates a mock web context when applicable but no real server port.
- **RANDOM_PORT** — starts an embedded server on an available port for real HTTP calls.
- **DEFINED_PORT** — starts a server on the configured port and can conflict with other processes.
- **NONE** — creates a non-web application context.
- **Client choice** — TestRestTemplate calls a running server; WebTestClient can be used either against a server or with supported direct bindings.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: @SpringBootTest has four web-environment modes. MOCK is the default and creates a mock web context when supported, but it does not open a network port. RANDOM_PORT and DEFINED_PORT start an embedded server; the former asks the operating system for an available port, while the latter uses the configured port. NONE creates a non-web context. I use RANDOM_PORT when the real HTTP boundary matters and MOCK when no socket is needed. TestRestTemplate needs a running server, while WebTestClient can also work with supported direct bindings, so the client is not defined solely by the mode.

questions.question: How does Spring Boot find the main application class when running a @SpringBootTest?
questions.title: How @SpringBootTest Finds the Main Class
questions.direct_answer: When no classes are supplied, Spring Boot searches upward from the test package for a class annotated with **@SpringBootConfiguration**; **@SpringBootApplication** includes that annotation. Keeping tests in the application package tree lets discovery work. Otherwise, set `@SpringBootTest(classes = MyApp.class)` explicitly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Spring Boot's component scanning and test context discovery mechanism
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting test classes in a different package tree than the main class and getting NoSuchBeanDefinitionException
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention you can explicitly specify the config class with @SpringBootTest(classes = MyApp.class) or use @ContextConfiguration

sections.title: How Spring Boot Discovers Your Main Application Class
sections.content:
When no `classes` value is supplied, Spring Boot searches upward from the test's package for a class annotated with **@SpringBootConfiguration**. **@SpringBootApplication** includes that annotation, so the main application class is normally found when tests live in the same package tree.

The discovered class becomes a source for Boot startup. Its component scanning, imports, exclusions, profiles, properties, and test customization determine the resulting context; discovery does not mean every class or bean in the project is loaded. If the test lives elsewhere or needs another source, use `@SpringBootTest(classes = MyApp.class)` explicitly.

sections.title: The Upward Search at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Start point|~Test package|com.example.app.web|search begins here|not the file-system directory
emerald|Walk upward|~Parent packages|com.example.app|look for @SpringBootConfiguration|@SpringBootApplication qualifies
amber|Found it|~Boot source|component scan and imports apply|test customizations still apply|context starts
rose|Not found|~Configuration error|Unable to find @SpringBootConfiguration|move under package tree|or set classes explicitly

sections.title: Correct Package Structure and Explicit Configuration
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Test class in unrelated package**: Freshers sometimes organize tests by test type rather than by component, putting all integration tests at com.company.integrationtests while the main class is at com.company.myapp — Spring Boot can't find the main class and the test fails with "Unable to find a @SpringBootConfiguration".
- **Renaming the main class package**: If you refactor your main class from com.oldname to com.newname but forget to update test package names, old tests suddenly can't find the application class.
- **Creating nested configuration in tests**: Some freshers create a @SpringBootConfiguration class inside their test class, which overrides the main application config and loads only that, missing all the real beans.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Upward scanning** — Spring Boot searches from the test package up through parent packages for @SpringBootApplication.
- **Standard structure** — main class at the root package, tests in the same package or sub-packages, ensures automatic discovery.
- **Explicit configuration** — use @SpringBootTest(classes = MyApp.class) when the test sits in a different package tree.
- **ComponentScan inheritance** — once the main class is found, its @ComponentScan rules decide which beans load.
- **Multi-module projects** — often need the explicit classes parameter because test and main live in different module roots.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: When you use the SpringBootTest annotation, Spring Boot needs to find your main application class — the one with the SpringBootApplication annotation — so it knows how to set up the context. It does this by starting at the package where your test class is and searching upward through the parent packages. So if your test is in com dot company dot myapp dot service, Spring Boot checks that package, then com dot company dot myapp, and so on, until it finds a class with the SpringBootApplication annotation. This is why the standard project structure works automatically — you put your main class at the root package like com dot company dot myapp, and your tests in the same package or sub-packages, and everything just works. The common mistake freshers make is organising tests by type rather than by component. Like putting all integration tests in com dot company dot integration tests while the main class is in com dot company dot myapp. Now Spring Boot can't find the main class because it's in a completely different package tree, and you get an error about being unable to find a Spring Boot configuration. The fix is either to restructure your packages, or to explicitly tell Spring Boot which class to use with the classes attribute on the SpringBootTest annotation. That overrides the automatic discovery and points directly to your main class.

questions.question: What is context caching in Spring Boot tests and why does it matter?
questions.title: Spring Test Context Caching
questions.direct_answer: The Spring TestContext framework caches an ApplicationContext under a key built from its configuration, including locations, classes, initializers, profiles, properties, customizers, and parent context. Tests with the same key can reuse it in the same process, avoiding another startup. The cache has a size limit, can evict entries, and is not shared across forked JVM processes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of Spring's test performance optimization and what configuration differences invalidate the cache
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @DirtiesContext broadly or varying test configuration unnecessarily, which reduces context-cache reuse
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain exactly what makes two contexts equivalent: same annotations, same properties, same active profiles, same classes parameter

sections.title: What Context Caching Is and Why It Exists
sections.content:
Creating a Spring application context can be one of the larger costs in an integration-test suite. The Spring TestContext framework therefore stores successfully loaded contexts in a static cache and lets later tests with the same cache key reuse them in the **same process**.

The key includes more than annotation text: configuration locations and classes, initializers, context customizers, the context loader, parent context, active profiles, test property sources, and dynamic properties can all contribute. A different key creates another cached context; @DirtiesContext removes the affected context. The cache also has a maximum size and can evict older entries, and a forked test process has a separate cache.

sections.title: What Makes or Breaks a Cache Hit
sections.content:
emerald|Cache hit|~Same TestContext key|same config classes|same profiles and properties|same customizers
rose|Another context|~Different cache key|different dynamic properties|different mocks or imports|separate process
blue|Removal|~@DirtiesContext|closes and evicts the context|later matching test rebuilds|scope depends on mode
amber|Limits|~Not permanent storage|bounded cache|older entries may be evicted|measure with cache logging

sections.title: Context Caching in Action
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @DirtiesContext everywhere**: It removes a reusable context from the cache, so later matching tests must create it again.
- **Varying configuration accidentally**: Different properties, profiles, dynamic-property values, imports, or context-customizing mocks can produce different keys.
- **Treating a context reset as database cleanup**: @DirtiesContext controls the application context. For database state, use a test-managed transaction when its boundary fits, or perform explicit cleanup.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Cache key** — Spring derives it from the full TestContext configuration, including classes, locations, profiles, properties, customizers, and parent context.
- **Process scope** — the static cache is shared only inside the same test process.
- **Bounded cache** — it has a maximum size and can evict older contexts.
- **Transactions are separate** — a test-managed @Transactional boundary may roll back compatible database work, but it does not define the context key.
- **@DirtiesContext** — removes and closes a context according to its configured mode; use it only for genuinely dirty context state.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Spring's TestContext framework caches an application context so another test with the same cache key can reuse it in the same process. The key includes configuration classes and locations, profiles, test properties, initializers, customizers, and any parent context. A different key means a different context; @DirtiesContext removes a context so it must be built again when next requested. The cache is bounded and is not shared across forked processes. I keep test configuration consistent when the tests need the same context, but I do not change behavior merely to chase a cache hit. For database isolation, a test-managed transaction can roll back work done inside its boundary; it is not a general replacement for cleanup or @DirtiesContext.

questions.question: How do you override application properties in a @SpringBootTest?
questions.title: Overriding Properties in @SpringBootTest
questions.direct_answer: Use `@SpringBootTest(properties = ...)` for inline test properties, `@TestPropertySource` for declared test sources, `@ActiveProfiles("test")` to activate profile-specific configuration, or `@DynamicPropertySource` for values created at test time. Spring has a defined property-source precedence, so use the mechanism whose scope and precedence match the test instead of assuming every test source is equivalent.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical knowledge of test configuration management, especially for changing database URLs, ports, or feature flags without touching production config
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating multiple application-test.yml files without understanding inline property overrides, or not knowing that test properties have higher precedence than application.yml
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention @DynamicPropertySource for runtime values such as container ports and avoid claiming a simple universal precedence between combined inline test mechanisms

sections.title: Overriding Properties in Spring Boot Tests
sections.content:
A Spring Boot test can supply values through `@SpringBootTest(properties = ...)`, `@TestPropertySource`, an active profile such as `test`, or `@DynamicPropertySource` for values known only at runtime. These mechanisms participate in Spring's Environment and have documented precedence over normal application sources, but combining several inline mechanisms for the same key makes intent harder to see.

Use one clear source for each scope: a profile for shared test defaults, an inline property for a class-specific case, and @DynamicPropertySource for values such as a Testcontainers port. Property overrides configure the test; they do not automatically create or isolate the external resource named by the property.

sections.title: Property Override Options at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|properties attribute|~Inline on @SpringBootTest|class-specific values|key=value entries|part of context cache key
emerald|@TestPropertySource|~Test property source|inline values or locations|core Spring support|clear scope
amber|@ActiveProfiles|~Select profiles|Boot can load application-test.yml|shared defaults|not itself an override value
rose|@DynamicPropertySource|~Runtime values|static registry method|container URL or port|higher precedence than @TestPropertySource

sections.title: Ways to Override Test Properties
Choosing the Right Tool for the Job
sections.content:
Use **@SpringBootTest properties** when you need to override 1-2 values quickly for a single test class, like changing a database URL or disabling a scheduler.

Use **@TestPropertySource** when you need more control, such as loading an external properties file or overriding many values with clear documentation.

Use **@ActiveProfiles("test")** when you have a consistent set of test-specific config shared across many test classes — this is the cleanest for teams, as all test config lives in application-test.yml and production stays in application.yml. For temporary overrides in a single test method, inject the **Environment** bean and read the value programmatically instead.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Duplicating all production configuration**: Override only what the test intentionally changes.
- **Assuming braces are mandatory**: Java permits the single-element shorthand for an array-valued annotation attribute, so both `properties = "a=b"` and `properties = {"a=b"}` are valid.
- **Setting one key in several test sources**: Even when precedence is documented, the result is harder to understand and cache reuse may change. Keep one obvious owner.
- **Hardcoding runtime ports**: Register container-generated values with @DynamicPropertySource.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **properties attribute** — supplies inline values for a @SpringBootTest class.
- **@TestPropertySource** — supplies inline values or property-file locations through Spring TestContext.
- **@ActiveProfiles("test")** — activates a profile; Boot can then load profile-specific application configuration.
- **@DynamicPropertySource** — registers runtime values and has higher precedence than @TestPropertySource.
- **Cache effect** — profiles, test properties, and dynamic-property customizers can affect the context cache key.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: I use @SpringBootTest properties for a class-specific inline value, @TestPropertySource for a declared test source, @ActiveProfiles to select shared profile configuration, and @DynamicPropertySource for runtime values such as a container URL or port. These feed Spring's Environment and override normal application sources according to the documented property order. I avoid setting the same key in several test mechanisms because the test becomes hard to read and may use a different context-cache key. I also remember that changing a URL only changes configuration; it does not itself start or isolate the database or service.

questions.question: What is the difference between @SpringBootTest and @ContextConfiguration in Spring?
questions.title: @SpringBootTest vs @ContextConfiguration
questions.direct_answer: **@SpringBootTest** uses Spring Boot's startup model and can discover the application's Boot configuration. **@ContextConfiguration** is the Spring TestContext annotation for declaring or detecting configuration classes, locations, initializers, and a context loader. It does not enable Boot auto-configuration by itself, although the classes you give it can import whatever configuration they need.

interviewer_intent.testing: Distinguishing Spring Boot features from core Spring Framework, showing awareness that Boot is a layer on top of Spring
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking they're equivalent or interchangeable, or not realizing @SpringBootTest is Boot-specific and won't work in plain Spring applications
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @SpringBootTest uses Boot's TestContext bootstrapper and SpringApplication, while @ContextConfiguration is the core TestContext configuration annotation

sections.title: Spring Boot vs Spring Framework Test Annotations
sections.content:
Both annotations participate in Spring's TestContext framework, but they express different levels of setup. **@SpringBootTest** uses Boot's test bootstrapper and **SpringApplication**. It can find the main Boot configuration, apply auto-configuration, and load Boot-style environment properties. **@ContextConfiguration** declares or detects configuration classes, XML or Groovy locations, initializers, and a context loader. It does not enable Boot auto-configuration by itself.

@ContextConfiguration does not require a list of every bean: a supplied configuration class may component-scan or import other configuration, and default configuration detection is also supported. In a Boot project, choose @SpringBootTest for broad Boot integration and use @ContextConfiguration when a deliberately defined Spring context is the real test boundary.

sections.title: @SpringBootTest vs @ContextConfiguration
sections.content:
| Aspect | @SpringBootTest | @ContextConfiguration |
|---|---|---|
| Layer | Spring Boot test support | Core Spring TestContext |
| Startup | Uses SpringApplication | Uses the selected context loader |
| Configuration | Can discover main Boot configuration | Classes or locations can be explicit or detected |
| Auto-configuration | Available through Boot configuration | Not enabled by the annotation alone |
| Properties | Boot test and application property mechanisms | Combine with @TestPropertySource or other property configuration when needed |

sections.title: Two Annotations, Two Layers
sections.content:
emerald|@SpringBootTest|~Boot integration|SpringApplication startup|main Boot configuration|Boot environment
blue|@ContextConfiguration|~Core TestContext|configuration classes or locations|initializers and loader|default detection supported
amber|Relationship|~Same testing framework|different bootstrap choices|can both create a context|not interchangeable promises
rose|Decision|~Match the boundary|broad Boot behavior|deliberately defined Spring context|prefer a slice when one exists

sections.title: Without Boot: @ContextConfiguration in a Boot app
With Boot: @SpringBootTest does the wiring for you
When to Use Each Annotation
sections.content: Use **@SpringBootTest** when the behavior depends on broad Boot startup, auto-configuration, and application wiring. Use **@ContextConfiguration** when the intended boundary is a specific Spring context or when testing a non-Boot Spring application. In a Boot application, a built-in slice such as @WebMvcTest or @DataJpaTest is often clearer when it matches the layer. A utility class that does not need Spring should normally use plain JUnit rather than either annotation.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **@SpringBootTest** — uses Boot's test bootstrapper and SpringApplication for broad Boot integration.
- **@ContextConfiguration** — configures a Spring TestContext with classes, locations, initializers, or detected defaults.
- **Auto-configuration** — comes from Boot configuration; @ContextConfiguration alone does not enable it.
- **Component scanning** — depends on the configuration classes supplied or discovered, not simply on the test annotation name.
- **Properties** — @SpringBootTest participates in Boot's property model; core Spring tests can use @TestPropertySource and other property mechanisms.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: @SpringBootTest is Boot-specific: it uses Boot's test bootstrapper and SpringApplication, can discover the main Boot configuration, and participates in Boot auto-configuration and property loading. @ContextConfiguration is the core Spring TestContext annotation for configuration classes, locations, initializers, and a context loader. It does not enable Boot auto-configuration by itself, but the configuration it loads may scan or import other beans, so it is not limited to one manually listed bean. I use @SpringBootTest for broad Boot behavior, @ContextConfiguration for an intentionally defined Spring context, and a built-in slice when the test needs only one supported layer.

questions.question: Can you use @Autowired in a @SpringBootTest class to inject beans?
questions.title: @Autowired in @SpringBootTest
questions.direct_answer: **Yes.** The Spring TestContext framework can inject beans from the test ApplicationContext into fields, setters, or constructors of the test instance. The test instance is managed by the testing framework with Spring support; it is not an ordinary application bean, and only beans present in that test context can be injected.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic Spring dependency injection knowledge applied to the test context, confirming they understand DI works the same way in tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking @Autowired doesn't work in tests or manually calling applicationContext.getBean() instead of using field injection
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that the TestContext framework prepares the test instance and can inject context beans; for context-level Mockito overrides, use current @MockitoBean or older Boot @MockBean

sections.title: Dependency Injection in Spring Boot Tests
sections.content:
With Spring's TestContext support, the test instance can receive beans from the test **ApplicationContext** through fields, setters, or constructors. Only beans that exist in that context are candidates for injection. The test class is prepared by the testing framework; it is not an ordinary application bean participating in all container callbacks.

For a context-level Mockito replacement, current Spring Framework provides **@MockitoBean**. Older Spring Boot versions commonly use **@MockBean**, which is deprecated in newer Boot versions. Both are different from plain Mockito **@Mock**, which creates a mock without registering it as a Spring bean.

sections.title: Injection Inside a Test, at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|Injection works|~From the test context|field or setter|constructor with test support|bean must exist
blue|Test instance|~Prepared by TestContext|not an application bean|listeners perform injection|lifecycle differs
amber|Context mock|~Replace a context bean|@MockitoBean current|@MockBean on older Boot|plain @Mock is not registered
rose|Skip the context|~Pure unit test|construct the subject directly|pass mocks to constructor|no Spring startup

sections.title: Autowiring Beans in Tests
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming any class can be injected**: @Autowired can only resolve a bean available in the test context.
- **Treating the test as an application bean**: TestContext prepares the test instance, but it does not make the class an ordinary application component.
- **Confusing @Mock with a bean override**: Use @MockitoBean in current Spring, or @MockBean on older Boot, when the mock must replace or provide a bean in the context.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Context-backed injection** — fields and setters can receive beans present in the test ApplicationContext.
- **Test preparation** — TestContext listeners prepare the test instance; the class is not an ordinary application bean.
- **Mockito bean override** — use @MockitoBean in current Spring or @MockBean on older Boot when a mock must live in the context.
- **Constructor injection** — supported with Spring's test constructor-autowiring rules.
- **Plain unit tests** — construct the class directly and use @Mock when no Spring context is needed.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Yes. Spring's TestContext framework can inject beans from the test ApplicationContext into the test instance. Field and setter injection are straightforward, and constructor injection is supported under the test-constructor rules. The requested bean must actually exist in that context. The test class is prepared by the testing framework rather than becoming an ordinary application bean. If one dependency must be replaced by a Mockito mock in the context, use current @MockitoBean or @MockBean on older Spring Boot versions. A plain @Mock is enough only when the test constructs the subject itself and does not need Spring.

questions.question: What is @DirtiesContext and when should you use it in a Spring Boot test?
questions.title: @DirtiesContext Explained
questions.direct_answer: **@DirtiesContext** marks a test ApplicationContext as dirty so the TestContext framework removes it from the cache and closes it. Depending on the configured class or method mode, this can happen before or after a test. Use it when a test changes context-level state that cannot be reset safely, because a later test may then have to build a new context.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Spring context lifecycle, context caching for performance, and the severe cost of context re-creation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding @DirtiesContext to every test class as a quick fix for test pollution, which destroys test suite performance by forcing context restarts
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the context caching mechanism and give a concrete example of when DirtiesContext is truly necessary versus when it's a code smell indicating bad test design

sections.title: Spring Context Lifecycle and @DirtiesContext
sections.content:
Spring's TestContext framework can cache an application context and reuse it for tests with the same cache key in the same process. **@DirtiesContext** tells that framework that the context is no longer safe to reuse. It closes and removes the affected context from the cache according to the configured before or after mode.

A later test requesting that key must create another context, so the cost depends on the application rather than a fixed number. Use the annotation when a test changes context-level state that cannot be restored safely. It is not a general database-cleanup annotation and should not be used merely to hide poor test isolation.

sections.title: @DirtiesContext at a Glance
sections.content:
rose|@DirtiesContext|~Evict and close|before or after modes|later matching test rebuilds|cost depends on context
blue|Why caching exists|~Reuse compatible contexts|same cache key|same process|bounded cache
emerald|Legitimate use|~Context cannot be restored|changed singleton state|closed context resource|modified bean definitions
amber|Try first|~Reset the real state|transaction when boundary fits|explicit data cleanup|restore a test double

sections.title: When @DirtiesContext Earns Its Cost (and the Cheaper Default)
Step 1: Identify If You Actually Need It
sections.content: Before using @DirtiesContext, ask whether the **application context itself** is unsafe to reuse. A test-managed @Transactional method normally rolls back database work performed on its transaction, but work committed by another thread or a real HTTP server is outside that boundary. HTTP requests can absolutely leave persistent state. Use explicit cleanup for external state; reserve @DirtiesContext for context-level changes such as a damaged singleton, modified bean definitions, or a closed resource owned by the context.

sections.title: Step 2: Choose the Right Scope
sections.content: @DirtiesContext can be placed on a test method or class. Method mode supports **BEFORE_METHOD** and **AFTER_METHOD**. Class mode supports **BEFORE_CLASS**, **BEFORE_EACH_TEST_METHOD**, **AFTER_EACH_TEST_METHOD**, and **AFTER_CLASS**. The defaults are AFTER_METHOD for a method and AFTER_CLASS for a class. Choose the narrowest mode that matches when the context becomes dirty; do not assume a before mode and an after mode have the same effect.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using it as a generic reset**: It resets a cached ApplicationContext, not every database, broker, file, or remote service.
- **Assuming @Transactional covers real-server requests**: A request handled on another thread uses a different transaction and may commit.
- **Ignoring the mode**: A class-level default acts after the class, while a method-level default acts after that method; before modes exist for different isolation needs.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Context-cache action** — @DirtiesContext closes and removes the affected ApplicationContext from the cache.
- **Variable cost** — a later test may need to recreate it; the time depends on the context.
- **Method modes** — BEFORE_METHOD or AFTER_METHOD, with AFTER_METHOD as the default.
- **Class modes** — BEFORE_CLASS, BEFORE_EACH_TEST_METHOD, AFTER_EACH_TEST_METHOD, or AFTER_CLASS, with AFTER_CLASS as the default.
- **Correct boundary** — use it for context-level state, not as a substitute for cleaning every external resource.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: @DirtiesContext tells Spring's TestContext framework that an ApplicationContext is no longer safe to reuse. Spring closes and evicts it according to the selected method or class mode, and a later test requesting that cache key creates another context. I use it only when the context itself has been changed or damaged and cannot be restored cleanly. It does not clean every external system. A test-managed transaction can roll back database work inside its boundary, but a real HTTP request running on another thread may commit independently. The method default is AFTER_METHOD and the class default is AFTER_CLASS; before and per-method class modes are available when that timing is required.
